title: Most Fares on a One-Way Drive
statement:
A driver goes along a road with stops numbered 1 to n, always moving forward from stop 1 toward stop n. Requests come as rides[i] = [start, end, tip]: carry someone from start to end (with start < end) and earn end − start + tip.

The car takes one ride at a time. A ride may begin at the same stop where the previous one ended. Choose any set of rides that fit and return the most money the driver can earn.

examples.why: Taking the two short rides earns (3 + 1) + (2 + 2) = 8. The single ride from 3 to 7 earns 4 + 10 = 14. Fitting in the most rides is not the goal.
Drop off at 3 and pick up at 3 right away: 2 + 3 = 5. The middle ride alone earns only 4.
Take 1 → 3 (2 + 4 = 6), then 5 → 9 (4 + 1 = 5). Taking 2 → 5 instead blocks the ride with the big tip.

hints: Let best[p] be the most you can have earned when the car is at stop p. How does best[p] relate to best[p − 1]?
Either no ride ends at p, so best[p] = best[p − 1], or some ride [s, p, t] is the last one taken, so best[p] = best[s] + (p − s + t).
Group rides by their end stop. Sweep p from 1 to n and fill best[p] from best[p − 1] and the rides that end at p. Every best[s] you need is already done because s < p.

explain.intuition:
This is weighted interval scheduling, made simpler because the positions are small integers. Ask: what is the most money in hand when the car reaches stop p? Either the car just rolled in empty, which is worth the same as at stop p − 1, or it just dropped someone off whose ride [s, p, tip] ended here. Then the earnings are whatever it had at stop s plus that ride's fare.

Greedy rules fail. The most rides (example 1) or the earliest finish (example 3) both pick worse sets. The table works because each choice is final: once the car passes a stop, nothing later can change what was possible before it.
steps: Put each ride into a bucket by its end stop.
For p from 2 to n: start with best[p] = best[p − 1].
For every ride [s, p, tip] in bucket p, set best[p] = max(best[p], best[s] + p − s + tip).
pitfalls: Using best[s − 1] instead of best[s]. A ride may start where the previous one ended.
Picking rides greedily by count, length or earliest end. Each fails on one of the examples.
Processing rides in input order instead of by end stop. Then best[s] may not be final yet when you read it.

solutions.title: Sort by end, check every earlier ride
solutions.idea: Sort rides by end. The best total ending with ride i is its fare plus the best total over any ride j that ends at or before ride i starts.

solutions.title: Sort by end + binary search
solutions.idea: Weighted interval scheduling: after sorting by end, binary-search the last ride that ends by the current start and take the better of skipping or using the ride.

solutions.title: Table over stops
solutions.idea: best[p] is the most earned on arrival at stop p: carry best[p − 1] forward, or finish a ride that ends at p.

followups: The road is 10⁹ stops long but there are still only 30 000 rides. Which version still works, and why?
The car has two seats, so up to two rides can overlap. How does the state change?
